mcqs.question: In the next-greater-element monotonic stack algorithm, why is the total time O(n) despite an inner `while` loop nested inside the outer scan?
options: The while loop never actually executes more than once total
Each index is pushed onto the stack exactly once and popped at most once across the entire run, bounding total pop operations by n
The algorithm secretly sorts the array first, then does one pass
It isn't O(n) — it's O(n²) but with a small constant factor
mcqs.explanation: Amortized analysis applies here: even though the while loop can pop several elements in one outer iteration, every element is pushed once and popped at most once over the whole algorithm, so total pop work across all iterations combined is bounded by n. There's no sorting step, and the bound is genuinely O(n), not a disguised O(n²).

mcqs.question: The daily-temperatures problem uses the exact same monotonic-stack skeleton as next-greater-element. What's the only thing that changes?
options: The payload recorded on each pop — the index distance instead of the value itself
The direction of the scan, from right-to-left instead of left-to-right
The stack must hold values instead of indices
The problem requires a completely different data structure
mcqs.explanation: Both problems scan left to right maintaining a decreasing stack of indices and pop on a strictly greater arrival — the only difference is what gets computed and stored when a pop happens: a value for next-greater, an index gap for daily temperatures. The scan direction, the choice to store indices, and the underlying structure are identical between the two.

mcqs.question: In the largest-rectangle-in-histogram algorithm, when a bar is popped because a shorter bar arrived, how is that popped bar's rectangle width determined?
options: It's always equal to the total number of bars in the histogram
It's fixed at exactly one bar wide
It requires a separate O(n) scan to find both boundaries
By the gap between the current index and whatever index is now left on top of the stack, since both boundaries are exactly the nearest shorter bars on each side
mcqs.explanation: The stack's remaining top (a shorter bar to the left) and the current index (a shorter bar to the right, the trigger for the pop) are exactly the two boundaries the rectangle can extend to — no extra scan needed, since the monotonic invariant already guarantees those are the nearest shorter bars. The width isn't fixed at one bar or the full histogram length.

mcqs.question: Why does the largest-rectangle-in-histogram algorithm append a sentinel value of 0 to the end of the input before scanning?
options: To make the array's length even
To speed up the algorithm from O(n) to O(log n)
To force every bar still left on the stack when input ends to be popped and have its rectangle resolved
To handle histograms containing negative heights
mcqs.explanation: Without a sentinel, bars still on the stack when the real input ends never trigger a pop and their rectangles are silently never computed — a sentinel guaranteed smaller than everything remaining forces a final flush. It has nothing to do with array length parity, doesn't change the algorithm's asymptotic complexity, and doesn't address negative heights, which the problem doesn't typically allow anyway.

mcqs.question: What is the core reason a monotonic stack turns an O(n²) brute-force scan into O(n)?
options: It sorts the input first, reducing the comparisons needed
It uses less memory than the brute-force approach in every case
No element is ever reconsidered after being popped — every comparison either advances the scan or permanently retires an element
It replaces comparisons with hashing
mcqs.explanation: The brute-force approach repeats work by rescanning from every starting index; the monotonic stack's invariant guarantees each element is examined a bounded number of times total (pushed once, popped at most once), eliminating that repetition entirely. It involves no sorting or hashing, and it typically uses more memory (O(n) for the stack) than a brute-force O(1)-space scan, not less.

mcqs.question: Why can switching the monotonic-stack pop condition from `<` to `<=` (or vice versa) silently break a solution rather than crash it?
options: It changes how ties (equal adjacent values) are resolved, which is a correctness question specific to what the problem statement wants, not something with one universally right answer
It only affects the algorithm's time complexity, not its correctness
It never changes the result — both comparisons are equivalent
It only matters when the input array is empty
mcqs.explanation: The strict-vs-inclusive comparison decides whether equal values trigger a pop, which changes duplicate handling in a way that depends entirely on what the specific problem wants for ties — there's no universal correct choice, which is exactly why this bug hides quietly until duplicate values appear in a test case. It's a correctness issue, not a complexity one, the two comparisons are not equivalent, and the effect has nothing to do with empty input.
